## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lecture, you will be able to:

::: {.incremental}
- Explain why statistical significance alone is insufficient for drawing conclusions
- Define p-hacking and identify researcher degrees of freedom
- Recognise HARKing and understand its implications for research credibility
- Describe the replication crisis and its causes
- Prepare effectively for the MCQ exam
:::

# Beyond p < .05 {background-color="#275882"}

## What Does p < .05 Actually Mean?

::: {.definition-box}
**p-value**: The probability of obtaining results at least as extreme as the observed results, assuming the null hypothesis is true.
:::

::: {.fragment}
What it does NOT mean:

- The probability that the null hypothesis is true
- The probability that your results are due to chance
- That your effect is important or meaningful
:::

## Statistical vs Practical Significance

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Statistical Significance**

- p < .05 threshold
- Depends on sample size
- Can be achieved with tiny effects
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Practical Significance**

- Effect size matters
- Real-world importance
- Clinical or applied relevance
:::

::::

## Effect Sizes Matter

::: {.concept-box}
A statistically significant result with a tiny effect size may not be meaningful in practice.
:::

- Cohen's d for group differences
- r for correlations
- Confidence intervals for precision

# P-hacking and Researcher Degrees of Freedom {background-color="#275882"}

## What is P-hacking?

::: {.definition-box}
**P-hacking**: The practice of collecting or selecting data or statistical analyses until non-significant results become significant.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Also known as:

- Data dredging
- Fishing expeditions
- Significance chasing
:::

## Researcher Degrees of Freedom

Decisions researchers make that can inflate false positive rates:

::: {.incremental}
- When to stop collecting data
- Which variables to include/exclude
- How to handle outliers
- Which statistical test to use
- Which comparisons to report
:::

## The Garden of Forking Paths

::: {.example-box}
**Example**: If you make 5 arbitrary decisions, each with 2 options, you have 32 possible analysis paths.
:::

::: {.fragment}
Many of these paths may produce p < .05 by chance alone.
:::

# HARKing {background-color="#275882"}

## What is HARKing?

::: {.definition-box}
**HARKing**: Hypothesizing After Results are Known - presenting post-hoc hypotheses as if they were a priori predictions.
:::

## Why is HARKing Problematic?

::: {.incremental}
- Confirmation bias masquerading as prediction
- Inflates apparent success of theories
- Makes research seem more compelling than it is
- Undermines the scientific method
:::

## Exploratory vs Confirmatory Research

:::: {.columns}

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Exploratory**

- Generating hypotheses
- Data-driven discovery
- Should be clearly labelled
:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Confirmatory**

- Testing pre-specified predictions
- Theory-driven
- Requires pre-registration
:::

::::

# The Replication Crisis {background-color="#275882"}

## What is the Replication Crisis?

::: {.concept-box}
Many published psychological findings fail to replicate when other researchers attempt to reproduce them.
:::

## Key Evidence

::: {.incremental}
- Open Science Collaboration (2015): Only 36% of psychology studies replicated
- Many textbook findings questioned
- High-profile retractions and fraud cases
:::

## Causes of the Crisis

- Publication bias (positive results only)
- P-hacking and flexible analyses
- HARKing
- Small sample sizes
- Underpowered studies
- Lack of pre-registration

## Solutions and Open Science

::: {.incremental}
- Pre-registration of studies
- Registered reports
- Open data and materials
- Replication studies valued
- Effect size reporting
- Larger sample sizes
:::
